turns.q:
Your response was: "Um, well, I—I noticed the way the totals are... I mean, the layout for the items is clear, but I'm not sure if the distinction between the prices is—sorry, that might be overthinking it. And then there’s the button area at the bottom; the "Continue Shopping" part feels very prominent, almost maybe too much? But again, I don't know if that's actually a design choice or just my own... well, I can't really say for sure. It's a lot to take in, so I—I might be misinterpreting the flow entirely."

We want to understand what you meant by "the "Continue Shopping" part feels very prominent, almost maybe too much?", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The “Continue Shopping” button is placed above “Place Order” in the bottom button area, making it appear higher in the visual hierarchy.

B) The “Continue Shopping” button takes up a full-width row and appears visually dominant compared with the payment form and bottom order controls.

C) The “Place Order” button appears visually muted below it, so the bottom area makes “Continue Shopping” look like the main action in the checkout layout.

D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
turns.a: C, I think. I mean, B is also true visually, and A maybe contributes, but the thing that stood out to me was that “Place Order” is greyed out and quiet while “Continue Shopping” is this strong black full-width button. So the checkout screen seems to be telling me the main thing to do is leave checkout, which feels… odd, unless the disabled state is temporary because the card fields are empty. But even then, I’m not sure the contrast should make the secondary action feel that primary.

turns.q: What specifically in the bottom area makes “Continue Shopping” read as the main action—the full-width shape, its position above “Place Order,” the dark fill, or the muted “Place Order” styling?
turns.a: The dark fill is probably the biggest part, I think, because it has the strongest contrast on the whole screen after the total amount. But its position makes it worse, maybe, because it comes first after the payment form, so my eye lands on it before I even process the grey “Place Order” button. The muted “Place Order” styling then confirms that it’s unavailable or less important, so the only actionable thing looks like “Continue Shopping.” I’m assuming that’s not intended, but if the order button is disabled until fields are filled, the secondary button maybe shouldn’t be the only high-emphasis control sitting there.

turns.q: If this layout were built exactly as shown, how would the dark “Continue Shopping” button being the only high-emphasis control affect someone’s understanding of what they’re supposed to do next in checkout?
turns.a: I think it would make the next step feel like “go back to browsing,” not complete payment, because that’s the only control that looks available and important. The actual checkout action is below it, but the grey makes it read as disabled, so unless the user already knows it will activate after filling the card fields, they might think checkout can’t continue yet—or worse, not notice that “Place Order” is the goal. Also, the small terms text under the disabled button kind of reinforces that “Place Order” belongs to the final legal step, but visually it’s so low-emphasis that it feels postponed. So I’d worry people fill the payment form and then maybe still hesitate, because the screen has trained them to look at the black button first, if that makes sense.

turns.q: Does the grey, low-emphasis “Place Order” below the black “Continue Shopping” make the checkout goal harder to locate, or harder to trust as the next step once someone sees it?
turns.a: Maybe both, but if I had to separate them, I’d say it’s harder to trust more than harder to locate. “Place Order” is visible, it’s just visually coded like it’s unavailable or not recommended, so even after I find it I’m not sure whether I’m supposed to be working toward it. The black “Continue Shopping” above it kind of feels like the safe, sanctioned action, while “Place Order” feels blocked or deferred. Sorry, I’m not saying users couldn’t figure it out, just that the hierarchy makes the final checkout action feel conditional in a way the screen doesn’t explain.

turns.q: What would someone need to infer from the grey “Place Order” and the empty payment fields to understand that completing checkout is still the intended path, despite the black “Continue Shopping” button dominating that area?
turns.a: They’d have to infer that “Place Order” is disabled only because the card fields are empty, and that the intended sequence is fill payment details first, then the grey button becomes active. But the screen doesn’t explicitly say that near the button, I don’t think, so you’re relying on people connecting the disabled styling with the blank fields above. And because “Continue Shopping” is already active and visually stronger, it kind of interrupts that inference with a competing path. Maybe a small validation hint or keeping the primary action visually primary-but-disabled would make that clearer, although I’m not completely sure how strict the style system is here.

turns.q: Would that visual hierarchy mainly cause someone to pause before completing the payment fields, or only create uncertainty after they’ve already connected the grey “Place Order” to the empty fields?
turns.a: I’d expect the pause to happen earlier, before they finish the fields, because the black button appears immediately after the payment card and looks like the next step after entering details, if that makes sense. It creates this weird moment where the form says “pay here,” but the first strong action says “continue shopping,” so a person might stop to re-evaluate the whole path rather than just fill and proceed. The grey “Place Order” only resolves if they already understand disabled checkout patterns, and I don’t know if everyone would make that connection quickly. So, maybe uncertainty after too, but the hierarchy is already interrupting them before that point, I think.

turns.q: What would that early pause change about how someone reads the Payment Details section and the intended path from the empty fields down to “Place Order”?
turns.a: It might make them read the Payment Details section less as “complete these fields to enable the order button” and more as just one optional block above a separate navigation choice, I think. The tiny card-type note under the fields is very low contrast, so there isn’t much there to guide the interpretation back toward “payment completion unlocks the next step.” If they pause at the black button, the vertical path kind of breaks: fields, then exit action, then disabled order action, instead of fields leading directly to order. I’d expect the fix to be, maybe, making “Place Order” the persistent primary position and putting “Continue Shopping” as a link or secondary outline below or above it, but sorry, that may be more prescriptive than you were asking.

turns.q: In this static layout, does that broken path make the payment section feel like part of checkout completion, or like a separate area that lacks a clear next step?
turns.a: It makes it feel a bit separate, I think, because the Payment Details card ends with that very faint “we accept…” line and then the next strong thing is not payment-related at all, it’s “Continue Shopping.” If the card visually contained the order action, or even if “Place Order” came immediately after the fields in the stronger position, I’d probably read the fields as leading somewhere. Here the white card closes, then there’s this black navigation button, then the actual order button is greyed out underneath, so the payment section feels like it just stops. I mean, the heading still says checkout, so it’s not totally lost, but the local flow under the fields is kind of… disconnected.

turns.q: What practical effect would that disconnected gap—payment fields ending, then the black “Continue Shopping,” then the grey “Place Order”—have on someone’s confidence about how to finish checkout from this layout?
turns.a: It would probably lower confidence because the screen makes them do a little reasoning step that maybe shouldn’t be necessary: “are these fields connected to that disabled button below the shopping button?” The big black “Continue Shopping” becomes like a divider between payment entry and completion, not just an option, so the path from card number to “Place Order” is visually interrupted. I’d especially worry that after entering details, someone might still look for a confirm action inside the Payment Details card or expect the grey button to change, but they have to kind of remember it’s below the unrelated black button. Maybe that’s obvious once interacted with, but in the static layout it feels like the finish action is detached from the task.

turns.q: Does that detachment make someone more likely to look for a missing checkout control near the payment fields, or more likely to assume the grey “Place Order” is intentionally unavailable for reasons the layout hasn’t explained?
turns.a: I’d lean toward assuming the grey “Place Order” is intentionally unavailable, because it’s visible and it’s in the expected bottom area, but the reason is kind of implied rather than stated. The missing-control feeling might happen inside the Payment Details card, maybe because the card just ends after that tiny “we accept…” text with no action or instruction. But since the disabled button is right there below, I think the bigger issue is someone has to diagnose why it’s disabled while the only active button sends them away. So it’s less “where is checkout?” and more “what condition have I not satisfied?”—sorry, that’s a small distinction, but I think it matters.

turns.q: What would that “what condition have I not satisfied?” question do to someone’s attention in this layout—would it keep them focused on the payment fields, or pull them down into decoding the grey “Place Order” area and the black “Continue Shopping” button?
turns.a: It would pull them downward, I think, because the unexplained state is at the button level, not inside the fields themselves. They might look back up at the empty card number and CVV, but only after first trying to understand why “Place Order” is grey and why “Continue Shopping” is the active-looking option. The issue is that the feedback, if it is feedback, isn’t attached to any specific field—there’s no required markers or inline message—so the user has to scan between the form and the bottom controls. And that scanning adds uncertainty right at the point where checkout should probably feel very linear, though I could be overstating it.

turns.q: How much does that need to scan between the empty payment fields and the bottom controls weaken the sense of a linear checkout path on this screen?
turns.a: Quite a bit, I think, because the screen is otherwise very vertical and simple: summary, payment fields, then action. But right at the action point, the order gets muddled by having the strongest button say “Continue Shopping,” so the eye has to jump back up and ask whether the empty fields are the reason “Place Order” is muted. There’s also no little cue like “complete payment details to place order” near the grey button, so the relationship is only inferred from layout, and the layout is fighting itself a bit. I mean, it’s not unusable, probably, but it weakens the checkout path at the most important handoff from entering data to confirming.

turns.q: What cue in this static layout would help someone connect the empty Payment Details fields to the muted “Place Order” button, instead of reading the black “Continue Shopping” row as the next step?
turns.a: Probably a line of text directly above or inside the muted “Place Order” area, like “Enter payment details to place order,” would do the most work, I think. Right now the only nearby explanatory text is the legal agreement below, which explains consequences after ordering, not why the button is grey. Even required markers on the Card number, MM/YY, CVV, and Name fields could help, but if the goal is connecting those fields to the disabled button, the cue has to sit near the button as well as the fields. Otherwise the black “Continue Shopping” still acts like this big visual full stop between the form and the intended checkout action, maybe.
